## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. The linear programming relaxation of the maximum weight matching problem on a bipartite graph $G=(V,E)$ with $V = U \cup W$ (with $|U| \neq |W|$) has an integral optimal solution.

**The LP relaxation.** Introduce a variable $x_e \in [0,1]$ for each edge $e \in E$. The standard LP relaxation of maximum weight matching is:

$$
\max \sum_{e \in E} w_e\, x_e
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
\sum_{e \in \delta(v)} x_e \le 1 \;\;\forall v \in V, \qquad x_e \ge 0.
$$

(Here $\delta(v)$ is the set of edges incident to vertex $v$.) This is the *fractional matching polytope*. We show every vertex of its feasible region is integral, so any LP optimum is attained at an integral point.

**Key tool: total unimodularity.** A matrix $A$ is *totally unimodular* (TU) if every square submatrix has determinant in $\{0, \pm 1\}$. The classic theorem of integrality states:

> If $A$ is TU and $b$ is integral, then the polyhedron $\{x \ge 0 : Ax \le b\}$ is integral — i.e., every vertex has all-integer coordinates.

**The incidence matrix of a bipartite graph is TU.** Let $A \in \{0,1\}^{|V| \times |E|}$ be the vertex-edge incidence matrix: $A_{v,e}=1$ iff $v$ is an endpoint of $e$. We verify the Ghouila-Houri criterion: a $\{0,\pm1\}$-matrix is TU iff every subset of rows can be partitioned into two classes (a "red/blue" signing) such that every column has its entries summing to $0$ or $\pm 1$ across the partition.

For a bipartite graph, take the natural partition of rows: color every vertex of $U$ red and every vertex of $W$ blue. Each edge $e = \{u,w\}$ with $u \in U$, $w \in W$ has exactly two $1$'s in column $e$ — one in a red row, one in a blue row. Assign $+1$ to red rows and $-1$ to blue rows; then each column sums to $+1 - 1 = 0$. The Ghouila-Houri criterion is satisfied (with the stronger property that every column sum is exactly $0$), so $A$ is TU.

**Crucially, this argument uses only bipartiteness — the partition $V = U \cup W$ with every edge crossing the cut. It does not require $|U| = |W|$.** The signing works column-by-column and is indifferent to the relative sizes of $U$ and $W$.

**Applying the integrality theorem.** The constraint matrix of the LP is exactly the incidence matrix $A$, and the right-hand side is $b = \mathbf{1}$ (all ones), which is integral. The nonnegativity constraints $x_e \ge 0$ are absorbed into the standard form $\{x \ge 0 : Ax \le b\}$. Since $A$ is TU and $b$ is integral, the feasible polytope

$$
P = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{|E|}_{\ge 0} : Ax \le \mathbf{1}\}
$$

is integral: every vertex of $P$ lies in $\{0,1\}^{|E|}$.

**Vertices correspond to matchings.** An integral point $x \in \{0,1\}^{|E|}$ satisfying $\sum_{e \in \delta(v)} x_e \le 1$ for all $v$ is exactly the indicator vector of a matching: each vertex is incident to at most one selected edge. Hence the vertices of $P$ are precisely the matchings of $G$.

**Conclusion.** A linear program attains its optimum at a vertex of the feasible polytope (provided the optimum is finite, which it is here since $P$ is bounded by $0 \le x_e \le 1$). Since every vertex of $P$ is integral and corresponds to a matching, the LP relaxation of maximum weight matching has an integral optimal solution — namely, an actual maximum weight matching.

**The condition $|U| \neq |W|$ is irrelevant.** The total unimodularity of the bipartite incidence matrix, and therefore the integrality of the matching polytope, holds for *every* bipartite graph regardless of the relative sizes of $U$ and $W$. The case $|U| = |W|$ (which yields the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem on doubly stochastic matrices as a special case) is not special — it is merely one instance of the same general phenomenon. When $|U| \neq |W|$, the maximum matching may be smaller than $\min(|U|,|W|)$ and the matching need not be perfect, but the LP optimum is still attained at an integral vertex.

Therefore, **yes**, the LP relaxation of the maximum weight matching problem on a bipartite graph with $|U| \neq |W|$ has integral solutions.

### PROOF COMPLETE
